notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Job 39. I was limited in the number of searches I could run, so the notes draw from the pages I was able to fetch and the rich excerpts returned from the searches. I have indicated where materials from particular traditions could not be located.

---

## General Overview of the Chapter

The consensus across all traditions consulted is that Job 39 completes God’s survey of animate creation begun at Job 38:39. Through a series of unanswerable rhetorical questions about wild animals — mountain goats, wild donkeys, wild oxen, ostriches, warhorses, hawks, and eagles — God demonstrates Job’s ignorance of and powerlessness over the natural world, which God alone governs with wisdom. The purpose is to humble Job and lead him to trust the God who orders creation so marvellously, rather than to demand explanations for his suffering.

**Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic):** God comes not as a harsh judge but as a “loving, winsome, vivid, powerful, humorous teacher.” The fact that God is once again in proper relation with Job is itself the answer, even without an explanation of suffering. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**Constable’s Expository Notes (Evangelical/DTS):** God asked Job more than 70 unanswerable questions. Since Job cannot understand God’s ways with nature, he cannot comprehend God’s dealings with people. It is wiser to bow in submission and adoration than to try to judge God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-39.html)

**Precept Austin (interdenominational evangelical):** The Lord’s speeches demonstrate that “the proper relationship between God and humankind (in all circumstances) is based solely on God’s sovereign grace and the human response of faith and submissive trust.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_commentaries)

**Pulpit Commentary:** “Throughout, the object is to show the infinite wisdom of God, and the utter incompetence of man to explain the mysteries of nature.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

**Gaebelein’s Annotated Bible (dispensational):** “Such a God is He whom Job has maligned… No answer could Job give. His silence is assent. God is great and unsearchable and Job but the rebellious worm of the dust.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/job-39.html)

**Peake’s Commentary (modern/critical):** “The point of the Divine speech throughout is that the world is not only for man: the poet takes refuge in this idea, which, however, involves a break with earlier religious conceptions.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-39.html)

---

## Verses 1–4: The Wild Mountain Goat and the Deer

**v. 1:** “Do you know when mountain goats give birth? Have you watched the doe bear her fawn?” — God asks Job if he knows the breeding and birthing times of the wild mountain goats (the ibex, Capra Sinaitica, also called yael sela, “wild goat of the rocks”) and the hinds (female deer). These creatures live on inaccessible rocky crags far from human observation. God alone oversees them.

- **Gill (Baptist/Reformed Baptist):** These goats dwell among rocks inaccessible to men; it is no wonder the time of their bringing forth is unknown to humans. The question is not about general knowledge but about the precise, providential oversight that belongs to God alone. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Asiatic ibex is “very shy and wild, difficult of approach,” inhabiting only the most rocky and desolate tracts. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** The providence of God is over wild creatures where no human pretence of care can be advanced. At their times of greatest need, God is present. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)
- **Benson (Methodist/Wesleyan):** Citing Chrysostom via Bochart, Benson notes it is remarkable that the wild goat, always in flight and leaping about, does not miscarry — only God’s wonderful providence preserves both dam and young. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

**v. 2:** “Can you count the months they are pregnant? Do you know the time they give birth?” — God alone numbers the gestation months and appoints the exact time of delivery.

- **Gill:** Hinds conceive after the rise of Arcturus (September) and go eight months; but “the exact time to a day and hour is not known.” If Job cannot know such common things in nature, how can he fathom the “womb of Providence”? (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 3:** “They crouch down and bring forth their young; they deliver their newborn.” — The hinds bow down (kneel) to give birth. The Hebrew verb for “bring forth” means to cleave or break through, describing the parting of the birth membranes. “They cast out their sorrows” refers to the afterbirth, or metonymically to the foetus itself.

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** “They bow down, they let their young break through, they cast off their pains.” The verb כרע (kara`) describes kneeling as the posture of one in travail (cf. 1 Sam 4:19). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)
- **Gill:** The hinds bring forth with great difficulty; nature provides helps — thunder to hasten birth (Ps 29:9) and the herb seselis to ease delivery. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 4:** “Their young ones thrive and grow up in the open field; they leave and do not return.” — The fawns grow strong rapidly and become independent, leaving the mother and not returning. God has engineered this cycle of maturity.

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** “They grow up with corn” — or more probably, “in the open field,” as the Hebrew word can mean. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** “The wild mountain goat teaches a lesson about growth and maturity engineered by God — Job didn’t design it or even understand it, yet it works perfectly.” Smick notes the ibex kid “can stand within minutes of birth and soon gambol off to thrive in the wild.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

---

## Verses 5–8: The Wild Donkey

**v. 5:** “Who set the wild donkey free? Who released the swift donkey from the harness?” — The wild donkey (Hebrew pere’, also called onager) is naturally free and untameable. The question is: who gave it this nature? Only God.

- **Gill:** Although wild donkeys can occasionally be tamed (Pliny notes some were), the creature “is naturally wild, is naturally averse to servitude.” God gave it this nature and desire for liberty. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** “One of the most admired animals of the Old Testament world was the wild donkey… The creature was admired for both its freedom and its ability to survive under the harshest conditions” (Smick). The angel’s declaration that Ishmael would be “a wild donkey of a man” (Gen 16:12) was a promise of enviable freedom. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**v. 6:** “I made the wilderness his home and the salt flats his dwelling.” — God appointed the barren wilderness and salt lands as the wild donkey’s habitat.

- **Gill:** The “barren land” is literally “salt land”; Pliny noted that wherever salt is, the land is barren. The deserts of Arabia were home to great numbers of these swift creatures. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 7:** “He scorns the tumult of the city and never hears the shouts of a driver.” — The wild donkey despises the noise and bustle of the city and will not heed a taskmaster’s shouts.

- **Ellicott:** The word for “driver” is the same as applied to the taskmasters of Egypt, raising the question “whether or not there may be a reminiscence of that bondage here.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Evangelical):** “It is better to labour and be good for something, than to ramble and be good for nothing. From the untameableness of this and other creatures, we may see, how unfit we are to give law to Providence, who cannot give law even to a wild ass’s colt.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

**v. 8:** “He roams the mountains for pasture, searching for any green thing.” — The wild donkey ranges widely over the mountains, searching diligently for whatever green vegetation can be found in the barren wilderness.

---

## Verses 9–12: The Wild Ox

**v. 9:** “Will the wild ox consent to serve you? Will he stay by your manger at night?” — The Hebrew re’em is not a “unicorn” (KJV), nor a rhinoceros, but the aurochs — an extinct, massive wild ox, the most powerful of all hoofed beasts. God asks whether Job can domesticate it.

- **Ellicott:** “It is a mistake to identify this animal with the rhinoceros, as was formerly done; it is more probably the same with the buffalo, or wild ox.” The contrast with the domestic ox shows the animal is not wholly dissimilar to oxen. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** “The beast in question is the aurochs, not the fabled ‘unicorn’ of the AV. Extinct since 1627, this enormous animal was the most powerful of all hoofed beasts, exceeded in size only by the hippopotamus and the elephant. It is the standard symbol of strength in the Old Testament” (Andersen). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)
- **Gill:** Taking the KJV’s “unicorn,” Gill discusses whether such a creature existed but leans toward the wild ox, noting that Strabo and Diodorus Siculus record abundant wild oxen among the Troglodytes near the Red Sea. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 10:** “Can you hold him to the furrow with a harness? Will he plow the valleys behind you?” — Job cannot yoke the wild ox to plough or harrow.

**v. 11:** “Can you rely on his great strength? Will you leave your hard work to him?” — Though immensely strong, the wild ox cannot be trusted with farm labour because he is unmanageable.

- **Gill:** “Tame oxen are employed because they are strong to labour… and they are to be trusted, in ploughing or treading out the corn, under direction, because they are manageable… but the wild ox, though stronger, and so fitter for labour, is yet not to be trusted, because unruly and unmanageable.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 12:** “Can you trust him to bring in your grain and gather it to your threshing floor?” — The climax: the wild ox cannot be relied upon to harvest grain.

- **Enduring Word:** God uses humour: “One might just as easily picture Job using a rhino to plow his field or put into his barn.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

---

## Verses 13–18: The Ostrich

**v. 13:** “The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully, but cannot match the pinions and feathers of the stork.” — The Hebrew is difficult. The traditional KJV rendered this as “Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich?” Modern translations and commentators largely agree the verse is about the ostrich alone, contrasting its beautiful but flight-incapable wings with the stork’s.

- **Ellicott:** “The wing of the ostrich is superb, but are her pinions and her feathers like the stork’s? Ostrich feathers are said to be worth from £8 to £15 a pound; but, beautiful and valuable as they are, they are hardly like the plumage of a bird, and are not so used for flight.” The ostrich runs like a quadruped, at up to fifty or sixty miles an hour. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Gill:** Argues the peacock is probably not intended, partly because it originated in India and may not have been known in Job’s Arabia. The ostrich was well known there, attested by Xenophon, Strabo, and Diodorus Siculus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 14:** “For she leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand.”

- **Ellicott:** “The ostrich only sits upon her eggs at night, when the cold would chill and destroy them; by day the heat of the sand continues the process of hatching.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Gill:** Some ancient writers believed the sun alone hatched ostrich eggs, but Gill notes the female does sit on them. Leo Africanus is cited: the female “lighting on these eggs, whether her own or another’s, sits on them and heats them.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 15:** “She forgets that a foot may crush them, or a wild animal may trample them.” — The ostrich seems careless, lacking instinct to protect her eggs.

- **Gill:** The ostrich may be forgetful of where she laid her eggs; she “forgets where it has laid them; and finding other eggs sits on them and hatches them, and regards the young as its own, and is hardened against its true and real young.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 16:** “She treats her young harshly, as if not her own, with no concern that her labor was in vain.” — The ostrich appears cruel and indifferent to her offspring.

- **Enduring Word:** “The seeming cruelty to her young derives from the practice of driving off the yearlings when mating season arrives” (Smick). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**v. 17:** “For God has deprived her of wisdom; He has not endowed her with understanding.” — God Himself made the ostrich this way — seemingly foolish, lacking the wisdom given to other creatures.

- **Enduring Word:** This is “the only real humor in the book of Job” (Mason). “It is what it is, a silly bird, because God made it so. Why? The comical account suggests that amid the profusion of creatures some were made to be useful to men, but some are there just for God’s entertainment and ours” (Andersen). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)
- **Gill:** Many ancient historians record the ostrich’s stupidity: it will eat stones and iron, thrust its head into a thicket thinking itself hidden, and be easily deceived by hunters. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**v. 18:** “Yet when she proudly spreads her wings, she laughs at the horse and its rider.” — Despite its foolishness, the ostrich can outrun a horse. When it rises to run, it “laughs” at pursuers.

- **Ellicott:** “She lifteth up herself” refers to when the ostrich sets out to run. Its habit of running in a curve is the only thing that enables horsemen to catch it. Ellicott also notes the possible alternative reading that the *stork* (not the ostrich) is the one who “laughs at the horse,” since the stork can truly fly and escape horsemen. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** “Get used to My absurdity, and live by faith rather than by sight. Be like the ostrich: though you cannot fly, you can still flap your wings joyfully!” (Mason). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

---

## Verses 19–25: The War Horse

**v. 19:** “Do you give strength to the horse or adorn his neck with a mane?” — God asks whether Job endowed the horse with its power and majestic appearance.

- **Ellicott:** “Thunder” (KJV “clothed his neck with thunder”) means “with terror, such as thunder causes. Some refer it to the moving or shaking of the mane.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** “Like many, Job could be impressed with the majestic strength of the horse. Yet he had no strength to give the horse; it came from God and not from Job or any other man.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)
- **Trapp (cited by Enduring Word):** “If the horse be so strong and warlike, what is the Almighty, that man of war?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**v. 20:** “Do you make him leap like a locust, striking terror with his proud snorting?”

- **Ellicott:** The phrase is better rendered “Hast thou made him to leap as a locust?” — not “Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper?” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)

**v. 21:** “He paws in the valley and rejoices in his strength; he charges into battle.”

- **Ellicott:** Notes the grammatical shift: “The first verb is plural, and the second singular. ‘They paw’ (literally, dig), and ‘he rejoiceth.’” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)

**vv. 22–23:** “He laughs at fear, frightened of nothing; he does not turn back from the sword. A quiver rattles at his side, along with a flashing spear and lance.” — The war horse is fearless, charging directly into armed combat without flinching.

**v. 24:** “Trembling with excitement, he devours the distance; he cannot stand still when the ram’s horn sounds.”

- **Ellicott:** The phrase rendered “Neither believeth he” (KJV) means “he disregardeth the summons of the trumpet, as though he did not believe that it gave the call to war.” That is, the horse does not believe the trumpet signals retreat — he charges on. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)

**v. 25:** “At the blast of the horn, he snorts with fervor. He catches the scent of battle from afar — the shouts of captains and the cry of war.” — The horse eagerly answers the trumpet with a snort (“Aha!”), smelling battle from a distance.

- **Ellicott:** “He saith among the trumpets” is literally “when there are plenty of trumpets: i.e., as often as the trumpet soundeth.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** Even the horse, the only domesticated animal in the list, retains a warrior nature that operates against reason and its own self-interest — Job cannot explain or control this. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)
- **Matthew Henry:** “The description of the war-horse helps to explain the character of presumptuous sinners. Every one turneth to his course, as the horse rushes into the battle. When a man’s heart is fully set in him to do evil… there is no making him fear the wrath of God.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

---

## Verses 26–30: The Hawk and the Eagle

**v. 26:** “Does the hawk take flight by your understanding and spread his wings toward the south?” — Job did not give the hawk its instinct for migration or flight.

- **Ellicott:** Notes that the more symmetrical literary order would place the ostrich after the war horse and before the hawk, providing a “gradual transition from the fleetest of quadrupeds to the fleetest of birds by means of the ostrich, which, though winged like a bird, cannot use its wings as birds do.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Enduring Word:** G. K. Chesterton observed that God describes all His creatures so that each one seems “like a monster walking in the sun. The whole is a sort of psalm or rhapsody of the sense of wonder. The maker of all things is astonished at the things He has Himself made.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**v. 27:** “Does the eagle soar at your command and make his nest on high?” — Job cannot command the eagle.

**v. 28:** “He dwells on a cliff and lodges there; his stronghold is on a rocky crag.” — The eagle nests in inaccessible rocky heights, beyond human reach.

**v. 29:** “From there he spies out food; his eyes see it from afar.” — The eagle’s keen vision is a gift from God, not from man.

**v. 30:** “His young ones feast on blood; and where the slain are, there he is.” — The eagle (or vulture-eagle) feeds on carcasses. This may be a grim image, but it too belongs to God’s ordering of nature.

- **Ellicott:** Notes the connection to Matthew 24:28 and Luke 17:37: “Where the slain are, there is she.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)
- **Gill:** “Where there has been a battle, and carcasses left on the field, the eagles will gather to them. This is particularly true of that kind of eagles called vulture eagles, as Aristotle and Pliny observe.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)
- **Precept Austin:** God “has created vultures with the instinct to feed on the wounded (including humans slain in battle — Job 39:30) to help prevent the spread of disease. Since Yahweh wisely supervises the balance of nature, which includes chaotic forces, humankind should trust him to restrict properly the chaotic and evil forces in society.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_commentaries)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On Job 39, the traditional readings from the commentaries consulted are remarkably unified. All agree the chapter’s purpose is to humble Job before God’s sovereign wisdom displayed in creation. There are no major doctrinal disputes over this chapter’s meaning. However, the following differences in **tone and emphasis** emerge:

**Reformed/Presbyterian (Barnes, preceptaustin.org):** Emphasises God’s sovereign providence over all creatures independent of man. Barnes stresses that “the providence of God is over them” and that at their times of greatest need, “God is present, and his care is seen in their preservation.” Precept Austin frames the whole as demonstrating that the proper relationship between God and man is “based solely on God’s sovereign grace and the human response of faith and submissive trust.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_commentaries)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill’s notes are heavily doctrinal and draw on classical natural history (Pliny, Aristotle, Aelian) to defend the literal truth of the text. His emphasis falls on God’s *particular* and *detailed* knowledge of each creature’s life cycle, contrasting it with man’s ignorance. He repeatedly concludes that if Job cannot understand these common things, he cannot fathom the “womb of Providence.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-39.html)

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Benson):** Benson draws on Bochart and Chrysostom to stress God’s *tender care* and *providential preservation* of the vulnerable. He highlights how the wild goat, constantly in flight, does not miscarry only because of God’s wonderful providence. The emphasis is on God’s compassionate oversight. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Guzik’s commentary uniquely highlights the *humour* and *personality* of God in this chapter — God as a “winsome, vivid, powerful, humorous teacher.” The ostrich section is read as “the only real humor in the book of Job,” and the application is relational: “God was once again with Job… and that was enough for Job.” The emphasis is on personal encounter with God rather than intellectual answers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-39/)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott’s notes are philologically precise, focused on translation issues (e.g., “unicorn” as mistranslation, the ostrich’s feathers, grammatical shifts in the Hebrew). His approach is scholarly and text-critical within an orthodox framework. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-39.html)

**Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Keil & Delitzsch provide thorough Hebrew exegesis, analysing verb forms (e.g., the Pilpel infinitive of חולל for travailing) and word meanings. They stress, with Bochart, that the knowledge in question is “not idle and merely speculative knowledge, but that knowledge which is proper to God, whereby He not only knows all things but also directs and governs them.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

**Puritan/Evangelical (Matthew Henry):** Henry draws moral applications not found in the other commentators — e.g., comparing the war horse to “presumptuous sinners” who rush into evil without fear, and the eagle nesting on high to sinners who “think themselves as safe in their sins as the eagle in her nest.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/39-1.htm)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

From the search results, **Peake’s Commentary** (modern critical) notes that the point of the Divine speeches is that “the world is not only for man,” an idea that “involves a break with earlier religious conceptions.” This is a thematic observation about the text’s theology of creation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-39.html)

**NET Bible notes** (referenced by Constable) state: “In the end the point is that Job cannot have the knowledge to make the assessments he made. It is wiser to bow in submission and adoration of God than to try to judge him.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-39.html)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

I was unable to fetch pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for Job 39 due to search and fetch limits. No Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this specific chapter could be accessed in this session.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching

No material on prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of Job 39 was found in the searches conducted.

---

## Summary Conclusion

All traditions agree: Job 39 is God’s classroom. Through unanswerable questions about creatures Job can neither understand nor control, God humbles Job and draws him from accusation to trust. The chapter does not explain Job’s suffering; it gives Job something greater — God Himself. As Enduring Word puts it: “His answer is Himself” (Mason). The differences between traditions lie not in competing interpretations of what the verses *mean*, but in the *tone* with which they are read — doctrinal precision (Gill), tender providence (Benson), grammatical exactness (Ellicott), homiletic moral application (Henry), or relational humour and encounter (Guzik).
